summary: Mobile IP tunnelling does not work through Network Address Translation devices. This memo adds extensions to Mobile IP and a tunnelling method that let mobile nodes operate in private address networks behind NATs. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3519 makes Mobile IP work through a NAT device. The trick is to carry the tunnelled traffic in UDP, using the same port numbers the registration already used, so the NAT's existing mapping sends the replies to the right place. The home agent recognises what has happened by noticing that the address a registration came from does not match the address in the registration itself, and then agrees to use the new tunnel.

questions: how does mobile ip work through nat

subtitle: A UDP-based tunnel that lets Mobile IP traffic pass through NAT devices that break ordinary IP-in-IP tunnels.

tldr.problem: Mobile IP assumes that every mobile node has a globally reachable address, and it tunnels traffic to that node inside IP-in-IP. A NAT device in the way rewrites addresses, and the IP-in-IP wrapper carries no port number, so the NAT cannot tell which mobile node a packet belongs to. Mobile IP therefore does not work at all across a NAT.
tldr.mechanism: The memo adds a UDP tunnel to the registration exchange. The mobile node offers to use it, the home agent sees that the source address of the request differs from the care-of address and agrees, and from then on data is wrapped in an outer IP header, a UDP header and a Mobile IP header. The ports are the ones already used for the registration, so the NAT's existing mapping carries the tunnel.
tldr.outcome: Three deployment cases are covered: a mobile node behind a NAT, a mobile node and foreign agent behind the same NAT, and a mobile node registering with a co-located address through a foreign agent that demands it. The cost is that the home agent has to trust an address it cannot authenticate, which opens a traffic redirection attack, so the memo recommends short registration lifetimes.

today: RFC 3519 is an Internet standards track document at the Proposed Standard level, and it has not been obsoleted. It extends the Mobile IP specification of RFC 3344, and the memo notes that it will fall out of use as IPv6 and Mobile IP v6 are deployed.

sections.title: The Problem
sections.content:
A basic assumption of Mobile IP, defined in RFC 3344, is that mobile nodes and foreign agents are uniquely identifiable by a globally routable IP address. That assumption breaks down when a mobile node tries to communicate from behind a NAT.

Mobile IP relies on sending traffic from the home network to the mobile node or the foreign agent through IP-in-IP tunnelling. IP nodes that communicate from behind a NAT are reachable only through the NAT's public addresses. IP-in-IP tunnelling does not generally hold enough information to permit a unique translation from the common public addresses to the particular care-of address of a mobile node or foreign agent behind the NAT, and in particular there are no TCP or UDP port numbers for a NAT to work with. For that reason IP-in-IP tunnels cannot in general pass through a NAT, and Mobile IP does not work across one.

The Mobile IP registration request and reply do pass through NATs, because they are UDP datagrams originated from inside the NAT. As they go out they make the NAT set up an address and port mapping through which the registration reply can come back in to the correct recipient. The problem is that the current Mobile IP protocol does not permit a registration where the mobile node's IP source address is neither the care-of address, the home address, nor 0.0.0.0, and a co-located care-of address behind a NAT is by definition a private address.

What is needed is an alternative data tunnelling mechanism that gives NAT devices the means to make unique mappings, and a registration mechanism that allows such a mechanism to be set up when appropriate. The memo addresses three scenarios: a mobile node with a co-located address behind a NAT and no foreign agent; a mobile node registered with a foreign agent where both the mobile node and the foreign agent are behind the same NAT; and a mobile node with a co-located address using a foreign agent that demands that registrations pass through it, by setting the R bit, where both are behind the same NAT.

The primary assumption of the document is that the network allows communication between a UDP port chosen by the mobile node and the home agent UDP port 434. If that does not hold, neither Mobile IP registration nor data tunnelling will work. The document does not assume that mobility is confined to a common IP address space; on the contrary, the routing fabric between the mobile node and the home agent may be partitioned into a private and a public network. The reverse tunnels considered are symmetric, using the same configuration, encapsulation method and IP address endpoints as the forward tunnel.
sections.plainLanguage: Mobile IP tunnels traffic to a mobile node using an IP-in-IP wrapper, and that wrapper has no port number in it. A NAT device has nothing to match on, so it cannot forward the traffic to the right mobile node. The memo's answer is to tunnel over UDP instead, so the NAT sees a normal port mapping, and to change the registration so the home agent accepts an address that does not match the one in the message.

sections.title: The Approach
sections.content:
In Mobile IP UDP tunnelling, the mobile node may use an extension in its registration request to indicate that it is able to use Mobile IP UDP tunnelling instead of standard Mobile IP tunnelling if the home agent sees that the registration request seems to have passed through a NAT. The home agent may then send a registration reply with an extension indicating acceptance or denial. Once the home agent has assented, UDP tunnelling is available for both forward and reverse tunnelling.

The ports are what make it work. UDP tunnelled packets sent by the mobile node use the same ports as the registration request message. The source port may vary between new registrations, but it stays the same for all tunnelled data and for re-registrations. The destination port is always 434. UDP tunnelled packets sent by the home agent use the same ports, but in reverse.

The sequence is therefore: the mobile node sends a registration request carrying the UDP tunnel request extension, the NAT creates a mapping for the reply as the request goes out, the home agent notices the discrepancy between the IP source address and the care-of address, and replies with a registration reply carrying the UDP tunnel reply extension. After that, any traffic from the home agent to the mobile node goes through the UDP tunnel. The mobile node may at its discretion use the UDP tunnel for reverse tunnelling or not, although in most cases where UDP tunnelling is needed, reverse tunnelling is needed as well.
sections.plainLanguage: The mobile node asks for the new tunnel in its registration, and the home agent answers in its reply. From then on the tunnel is just a UDP flow to a port the NAT already has a mapping for, which is port 434 at the home agent.

sections.title: The New Message Formats
sections.content:
The UDP Tunnel Request extension is a skippable extension carried in the registration request. It signifies that the sender can handle Mobile IP UDP tunnelling, and optionally that a particular encapsulation format is requested. It has type 144 and a length of 6 bytes, not counting the type and length bytes, and a sub-type of 0. It carries three reserved fields that must be set to zero on sending, of which the third must be verified as zero on receipt or the extension is handled as not understood and silently skipped. That last rule permits future additions that either coexist with old implementations or force a rejection.

Two flags matter. The F, or Force, flag says the mobile node wants Mobile IP UDP tunnelling established regardless of the outcome of the NAT detection performed by the home agent, which is useful when the route between the mobile node and the home agent works for signalling packets but not for generic data, for instance because of firewall filtering rules. If the home agent supports the protocol it should either accept the traversal and reply with a UDP tunnel reply extension, or reject the registration request, and in the latter case it should send a registration reply with the code field set to 129, administratively prohibited. If the home agent does not understand the extension it discards it silently and replies with code 0, registration accepted, but without the reply extension, and in that case the mobile node must not use UDP tunnelling. The R, or Registration through FA Required, flag says the R bit was set in the foreign agent's agent advertisement, and that registration is being made using a co-located care-of address but through the foreign agent.

The Encapsulation field gives the type of tunnelled data, using the same numbering as the IP header protocol field: 4 for an IP header, that is IP-in-UDP tunnelling; 47 for a GRE header, GRE-in-UDP tunnelling; and 55 for the minimal IP encapsulation header. If the home agent finds that UDP tunnelling is not needed, the encapsulation is determined by the M and G flags of the registration request. If it finds that UDP tunnelling should be done, the encapsulation comes from the Encapsulation field, and a value of zero means the M and G flags decide.

When the mobile node requests UDP tunnelling the D bit, decapsulation by the mobile node, must be set, or the tunnelling would not be meaningful. Both the mobile node and the foreign agent should set the T bit when requesting UDP tunnelling, even if not all traffic will be reverse tunnelled, so that a home agent not prepared to accept reverse tunnelling will not accept a registration that turns out to be unusable.

The UDP Tunnel Reply extension is a non-skippable extension sent in reply to a request extension. It has type 44, a length of 6 bytes and a sub-type of 0. Its reply code says whether the home agent will use UDP tunnelling for the current mobility binding: values from 0 to 63 mean assent and tunnelling will be done, values from 64 to 255 mean it should not be done. Two codes are defined, 0 for will do tunnelling and 64 for tunnelling declined, reason unspecified. The extension also carries the F flag, set when tunnelling is being forced because the F flag was set in the request, and a keepalive interval giving the interval the mobile node should use, with a value of 0 meaning the mobile node must use its own default.

The MIP Tunnel Data Message header, of type 4, serves to tell traffic tunnelled through the well-known port 434 apart from other Mobile IP messages such as registration requests and replies. Its next header field gives the type of tunnelled data, using the same numbering as the IP header protocol field. The receiver must check that the next header value matches the tunnelling mode established for the mobility binding the packet was sent with, and must drop the packet if a discrepancy is detected.

A new flag, U, is added to the agent advertisement of a foreign agent to say that it supports Mobile IP UDP tunnelling. It should be set in advertisements from a foreign agent that supports the tunnelling and is behind a NAT, and must not be set in advertisements from foreign agents that are not behind a NAT.

Finally, one new registration reply code is defined, ERROR_HA_UDP_ENCAP_UNAVAIL, requested UDP tunnel encapsulation unavailable, which lets the home agent distinguish a denial caused by an unavailable UDP tunnel encapsulation mode from one caused by unavailable standard tunnel encapsulation requested with the T bit together with the M or G bit.
sections.plainLanguage: Two new extension blocks are added to the registration messages. The one in the request says the mobile node can use the UDP tunnel and may name the encapsulation it wants. The one in the reply says the home agent agrees, gives the keepalive interval, and the home agent also adds a flag to its agent advertisements when it is behind a NAT itself.

sections.title: Encapsulation and Decapsulation
sections.content:
The default encapsulation mode for Mobile IP UDP tunnelling is IP-in-UDP. Any home agent and mobile node that implements Mobile IP UDP tunnelling must implement it. The mobile node may request alternative forms by setting the M bit and the G bit of a registration request, or by naming a particular encapsulation in the Encapsulation field. If the G bit is set and the Encapsulation field is zero, the mobile node asks for GRE encapsulation, and if UDP tunnelling is also requested and accepted, GRE-in-UDP is used in the same cases as GRE in IP would have been. If the M bit is set and the Encapsulation field is zero, the mobile node asks for minimal encapsulation, and minimal encapsulation in UDP is used in the same cases as minimal encapsulation would have been. When the Encapsulation field is non-zero it names a particular format, and the request must either be accepted with that encapsulation or rejected with the error code ERROR_HA_UDP_ENCAP_UNAVAIL, after which the mobile node may send a new registration request with different requirements.

Mobile IP IP-in-UDP tunnelling is done in a manner analogous to IP-in-IP tunnelling, with the addition of a UDP header and a Mobile IP message header between the outer and the inner IP header. An outer IP header, UDP header and Mobile IP message header are inserted before the datagram's existing IP header. The outer IP header's source and destination addresses, together with the UDP header's source and destination ports, identify the endpoints of the tunnel. The inner IP header's addresses identify the original sender and recipient, and the inner header is not changed by the encapsulator except to decrement the TTL by one when the tunnelling is part of forwarding, and it stays unchanged during delivery to the tunnel exit point.

Registration requests and replies are already UDP messages and must not be tunnelled, even when IP-in-UDP tunnelling is in force. Minimal encapsulation and GRE encapsulation are done in an analogous manner, using outer IP, UDP and Mobile IP headers in place of the outer IP header.

Before decapsulation is done, the decapsulating node must verify that the outer IP addresses and the UDP port numbers exactly match the values used for the tunnel, except for half bound tunnels where the source UDP port can change. IP-in-UDP traffic is decapsulated by stripping off the outer IP, UDP and Mobile IP headers, which leaves the original IP packet, which is forwarded as it is. Minimal IP encapsulation is processed in three steps: the UDP and Mobile IP headers are removed and the protocol field of the IP header replaced with the next header field of the Mobile IP tunnel data header; the remaining IP header's total length and checksum are adjusted to match the stripped packet; and ordinary minimal IP encapsulation processing is done.
sections.plainLanguage: Tunnelled traffic gets an outer IP header, a UDP header and a small Mobile IP header in front of the original packet. The addresses and ports on the outside name the tunnel, and the packet inside keeps the addresses of the real sender and receiver. On arrival the outer headers are checked against the tunnel and then stripped off.

sections.title: What Each Party Does
sections.content:
The mobile node. The UDP tunnel request extension may be used in a registration request when the mobile node uses a co-located care-of address, and must not be used when it is registering with a foreign agent care-of address. Its purpose is to indicate to the home agent that the mobile node can accept UDP tunnelling if the home agent has an indication that the mobile node resides behind a NAT, so it works as a conditional solicitation for the traversal. The extension must be placed before the Mobile-Home authentication extension in registration messages, so that it is covered by that authentication extension. If the mobile node includes the request extension and receives a reply without a reply extension, it must assume the home agent does not understand the extension and must not use UDP tunnelling. When it sends tunnelled data it must use the same UDP source port as the most recent registration request, and on re-registration without moving it should take care to use the same source port as the original registration of the current binding, or packets in flight will be dropped at the old port.

If the mobile node registers through a foreign agent using a co-located care-of address and the agent advertisement had the U bit set, the mobile node must set the R flag in its request extension so that the home agent uses UDP tunnelling, and it must also send a keepalive as soon as its registration is accepted. If the advertisement did not have the U bit set, the mobile node must not include the request extension at all.

The foreign agent. The foreign agent may use the request extension when forwarding a registration request to the home agent, if it is behind a NAT or has some other compelling reason to require UDP tunnelling. When it does so it must send the registration request with an IP source address matching the care-of address, because the home agent detects a NAT by seeing a mismatch between the source address and the care-of address. A foreign agent that requires the mobile node to register through it by setting the R bit must not add the request extension when forwarding a registration that uses a co-located care-of address, because that would set up a UDP tunnel to the foreign agent instead of to the mobile node. When the foreign agent shares a mobility security association with the home agent and appends a Foreign-Home authentication extension, the request extension must be placed before it.

A foreign agent behind a NAT may be configured to encourage reverse tunnelling or to be neutral about it, depending on the NAT. If the NAT translates all source addresses of outgoing packets to its own public address, sessions cannot be maintained when moving away from the network if the mobile node used triangular routing instead of reverse tunnelling. If it is known that the NAT is smart enough not to translate publicly routable source addresses and does no ingress filtering, triangular routing may succeed, and the leg from the home agent to the foreign agent will still use UDP tunnelling. So if it is known that the NAT will translate public as well as private addresses, or that ingress filtering is being done, the foreign agent should reply to registration requests that do not have the T bit set with reply code 75, reverse tunnel is mandatory and T bit not set. If the behaviour of the NAT is unknown, it should be assumed that it will translate all addresses, and the same reply applies.

The home agent. The home agent must use a mismatch between the source IP address and the care-of address in the registration request as the indication that the mobile node may reside behind a NAT. If the request also contains the request extension without the R flag set, and the home agent is capable of and permits UDP tunnelling, it shall respond with a registration reply containing an assenting reply extension. If the request has a matching source address and a co-located care-of address but contains the extension, the home agent should respond with a declining reply, unless tunnelling was explicitly requested with the F flag.

If the home agent assents to UDP tunnelling it must use the source address of the registration request as the effective care-of address, rather than the care-of address given in the request, except where the R flag is set. With the R flag set, the source address and port of the request may be a NAT'ed version of the foreign agent's address and port, so to direct traffic correctly the home agent must wait for the first keepalive from the mobile node before it can send traffic back to the correct NAT port. It must check that the outer source address, but not the port, of that keepalive is identical to the source address of the corresponding registration request, and that the inner source address is the home address of the mobile node and the inner destination address is that of the home agent. If all that holds, the outer source address and port of the keepalive are used as the outer destination address and port of the tunnel.

The home agent should be consistent in acknowledging support for UDP tunnelling or not, so a home agent that understands the request extension and is prepared to respond positively should also respond with a declining reply code when tunnelling is not indicated. The mobile node must not assume that behaviour, since the home agent may undergo a software change with reboot, a policy change or a replacement.
sections.plainLanguage: The mobile node offers the tunnel in its registration and the home agent decides. The home agent spots a NAT by noticing that the address the request came from is not the address in the request, and if it agrees it uses that address as the real care-of address. A foreign agent behind a NAT may add the same offer when it forwards a registration, and may insist on reverse tunnelling if the NAT rewrites every address it sees.

sections.title: Keepalives and Losing the NAT Mapping
sections.content:
The existence of the bidirectional UDP tunnel through the NAT depends on the NAT keeping state information associated with a session, and because the NAT may decide that a session has terminated after a certain time, keepalive messages may be needed to keep the tunnel open. The keepalives should be sent more often than the timeout the NAT uses, which may be assumed to be a couple of minutes according to RFC 2663, though shorter timeouts may exist in some NATs. That is why the extension used to set up the UDP tunnel can set the keepalive interval to another value than the default.

The keepalive message must consist of a properly UDP encapsulated ICMP echo request directed to the home agent. For each mobility binding with UDP tunnelling established, the non-home-agent endpoint must send a keepalive if no other packet to the home agent has been sent in K seconds, where K is a parameter with a default value of 110 seconds that the home agent may set to another value in the reply extension. The first keepalive is sent at the earliest K seconds after the registration request was sent, and the same UDP source port must be used for the keepalives as for the original registration messages and for data messages.

The remote tunnel endpoint must use two-way keepalives, consisting of UDP encapsulated ICMP echo request and reply messages, for two reasons. Two-way keepalives let the mobile node detect the loss of a NAT mapping, which in turn lets it compensate by re-registering and using a shorter keepalive to avoid losing mappings in the future. And one-way keepalives actually cause more keepalive traffic overhead, because the messages have to be sent more frequently to compensate for occasional loss, whereas two-way keepalives are acknowledged and retransmissions occur only when a response is not received within a reasonable time.

When a mobile node does not get a reply to its encapsulated echo request even after a number of retransmissions, and is still connected to the same router that was used to establish the current mobility binding, it should re-register with the home agent. That lets the home agent know about the new NAT mapping and restores connectivity. The point is not the loss of the mapping itself but that the home agent, in the absence of a registration request through the new mapping, will keep sending traffic to the NAT port of the old mapping.

Having established a new mobility binding, the mobile node may use a shorter keepalive interval than before, and may deviate from the interval assigned by the home agent. If the binding loss continues, it may shorten the interval each time it re-registers, until it reaches one that keeps the mapping alive. The strategy is implementation dependent, but the mobile node must not use a keepalive of less than 10 seconds. This only applies while the mobile node re-registers through the same router and therefore presumably through the same NAT device; if the mobile node moves and still finds itself behind a NAT it should return to its original keepalive interval and should not do any compensation unless it discovers a loss of mapping in the new environment.

The home agent must not try to detect or compensate for the loss by dynamically changing the keepalive interval it assigned in the registration reply, because it does not have enough information to do it reliably. The mobile node is in a much better position to tell when a mapping has actually been lost. A mobile node is also allowed to let a mapping expire if it no longer needs connectivity.

For a foreign agent behind a NAT, the same discussion applies only in a limited sense, and the answer is to configure the foreign agent permanently with a keepalive interval lower than the NAT mapping lifetime rather than trying to adapt dynamically.
sections.plainLanguage: The NAT forgets a mapping after a while, and the tunnel dies with it. The mobile node therefore sends an echo request inside the tunnel every so often, by default every 110 seconds, and the home agent answers. If the answer stops coming, the mobile node re-registers so that the home agent learns the new port, and it may then send its keepalives more often, but never less than every 10 seconds.

sections.title: Implementation Issues
sections.content:
Giving a mobile node a way to traverse NATs with Mobile IP traffic expands the address space where a mobile node may function and acquire care-of addresses, and with it comes a new problem of movement detection and address aliasing.

Because private networks use overlapping address spaces, they may be mistaken for one another in some situations, which the document calls private address aliasing. A mobile node implementing this specification may therefore need to monitor the link layer address of the gateway it sends packets through. A change in the link layer address indicates probable movement to a new network, even if the IP address remains reachable. The memo's example: a mobile node obtains the co-located care-of address 10.0.0.1, netmask 255.0.0.0 and gateway 10.255.255.254 by DHCP from one network, then moves to a network with an identical addressing scheme where the only difference is the gateway's link layer address. The mobile node should store the link layer address it first obtains, using ARP for instance, and detect changes in successive ARP exchanges as part of its ordinary movement detection. In rare cases a mobile node may not be able to monitor the link layer address and may confuse one point of attachment with another, and the document does not address that case; the traffic blackout it can cause may be limited by keeping the mobility binding lifetime short enough, since the re-registration caused by expiry fixes the problem.

On the lifetime itself, the home agent is allowed to decrease the lifetime indicated in the registration request. When using UDP tunnelling a short lifetime is beneficial in two cases. If the NAT mapping is dropped a connection blackout arises: new packets from the mobile node or foreign agent will establish a new NAT mapping, which the home agent will not recognise until a new mobility binding is established by a new registration request. And if the mobile node cannot detect mobility and ends up behind a new NAT device, a short lifetime keeps the blackout from lasting too long. What counts as short depends on the scenario; the suggested maximum lifetime returned by the home agent is 60 seconds, but longer lifetimes may of course be used where those scenarios are not a concern.
sections.plainLanguage: Behind a NAT, the mobile node's address is private, and two private networks can look alike. The memo suggests the mobile node watch the hardware address of its gateway to tell that it has moved, and it suggests the home agent hand out short registration lifetimes, so that a lost NAT mapping does not cause a long outage.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The ordinary Mobile IP security mechanisms are also used with the NAT traversal mechanism, but there is one noticeable change: the mechanism requires the home agent to trust unauthenticated address and port fields that NATs may have modified.

Relying on unauthenticated address information when forming or updating a mobility binding leads to redirection attack vulnerabilities. An attacker may do what NATs do, that is modify addresses and ports and so cause traffic to be redirected to a chosen address, and the same vulnerabilities apply to both mobile-node to home-agent and foreign-agent to home-agent NAT traversal. Without a NAT, the care-of address in the registration request is used directly by the home agent to send traffic back, and it is protected by the mobile-home or foreign-home authentication extension. Across a NAT, the effective care-of address from the home agent's point of view is that of the NAT, which is not protected by any authentication extension but inferred from the apparent IP source address of the received packets. Using the registration extensions to enable NAT traversal therefore opens one up to having the care-of address of a mobile node or foreign agent maliciously changed by an attacker.

Some, but not all, of the attacks could be alleviated to some extent by a simple routability check, but the document does not specify such a mechanism, for simplicity and because it would not protect against all redirection attacks. To limit how long such an attack can last, the memo recommends a conservative, that is short, mobility binding lifetime when using the NAT traversal mechanism.

Two specific attacks are described. An attacker on the route between the mobile node or foreign agent and the home agent may redirect mobility bindings to a desired address simply by modifying the IP and UDP headers of the registration request. Having modified the binding, the attacker no longer needs to listen to or manipulate the traffic, and the redirection is in force until the mobility binding expires or the mobile node re-registers. This may be used to read traffic destined for a mobile node, to send traffic impersonating the mobile node, or to redirect traffic to a victim host to cause denial of service on that host. The only defence is a short time between re-registrations, which limits how long the redirection lasts after the attacker has stopped modifying the messages.

The second attack opens up when registering through a foreign agent using a co-located care-of address. After the registration exchange, the mobile node is expected to send the first keepalive, and the binding stays in a half bound state until it arrives. An attacker who has observed the exchange may send a bogus keepalive assuming that state, which opens a similar redirection attack, and the attacker does not need to modify packets in flight, only to observe them. The home agent must therefore not accept a keepalive from a different source IP address than the one the registration request came from, which limits the attack to redirecting traffic to a bogus UDP port. The other defences are a short time between re-registrations and minimising the time the binding is half bound by having the mobile node send the first keepalive immediately after receiving an affirmative registration reply.

For IPsec, if the intermediate network is considered insecure it is recommended that IPsec be used to protect user data traffic, but IPsec does not protect against the redirection attacks, other than to protect the confidentiality of hijacked user data. The mechanism does allow all IPsec-related traffic to go through NATs without any modification to IPsec, and the IPsec security associations do not need to be re-established when the mobile node moves.

The document does not specify a general firewall traversal mechanism, but the mechanism makes it possible to use a single address and port for all mobile-node to home-agent or foreign-agent to home-agent communication, and using the same port for the tunnelled traffic as for the control messages makes it quite probable that if a registration can reach the home agent, the tunnelling will also work.
sections.plainLanguage: The price of this scheme is that the home agent has to believe an address it cannot check, because the NAT rewrote it. An attacker on the path can rewrite it too, and then the mobile node's traffic goes to the attacker. The memo says the only real defence is to re-register often, so that a hijacked binding does not last long.

items.desc: The home agent assents. Values from 0 to 63 mean tunnelling will be done.

items.label: Tunnelling declined
items.desc: Reason unspecified. Values from 64 to 255 mean tunnelling should not be done.

items.label: Reverse tunnel mandatory
items.desc: The foreign agent's reply when a registration lacks the T bit and the NAT needs reverse tunnelling.

items.label: Administratively prohibited
items.desc: The home agent's reply when traversal is detected but not allowed, or when forced traversal is not permitted.

items.label: Poorly formed Request
items.desc: The home agent's reply when the extension is malformed, for example when the D bit is wrong or a reserved field is nonzero.
